strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clinically important gap: general MLLMs lack quantitative analysis and rigorous, criteria-based reasoning needed for medical diagnosis.

The hierarchical task-level (RAG-based planning) and case-level (tool-based execution) design is a sensible way to combine LLM reasoning with specialized medical vision tools (segmentation, classification, VQA) and produces interpretable, evidence-linked outputs.

Reports substantial quantitative improvements over general MLLM baselines (GPT-4o, LLaVa-Med, Janus-Pro) and even outperforms REFUGE2 challenge winners and fine-tuned ophthalmology MLLMs on the glaucoma task.
Includes an informative ablation study analyzing the contribution and interaction of individual clinical indicators and comparing MOE vs. LLM decider strategies.
The case study (Figure 3) offers a transparent, step-by-step trace of the agentic workflow that illustrates how evidence is aggregated, supporting the interpretability claim.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to only two diseases/datasets (glaucoma on REFUGE2 with 1200 images, heart disease on MITEA reduced to binary classification from 536 images/143 subjects), which is a narrow basis for claims of general 'multi-modal medical diagnosis' capability.
The heart-disease task is oversimplified from a 7-class problem to binary classification due to limited data, reducing clinical relevance and making comparisons less informative.

The MOE decider's weights and threshold (θ) determination process is not clearly described or validated (e.g., no train/val/test split, cross-validation, or sensitivity analysis), raising concern about possible tuning on the test set and about reproducibility.

Comparisons to general MLLMs (GPT-4o, LLaVa-Med) as baselines are somewhat unfair/strawman, since these models were never designed to perform quantitative image analysis or use external tools; the performance gain largely stems from plugging in specialized segmentation/classification tools rather than from the proposed agentic reasoning workflow itself. No ablation isolates the benefit of the LLM-driven planning/orchestration versus a simpler fixed pipeline using the same tools.

Missing comparisons against other existing medical agentic frameworks explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., MDAgents, MedAgents, MMedAgent, MedRAX), which would better contextualize the contribution relative to prior agent-based approaches.

Despite claiming a 'zero-shot' or fine-tuning-free advantage, the framework relies on task-specific trained segmentation adapters (e.g., optic cup/disc, myocardium) and curated toolboxes/knowledge bases per disease, which somewhat undercuts the generality/zero-shot narrative and requires significant engineering effort per new disease.
No human expert (clinician) evaluation of the generated explanations or diagnostic evidence, despite interpretability/reliability being highlighted as a primary contribution.
Limited statistical rigor: no variance/confidence intervals reported for the main results (aside from repeated slice sampling for 3D heart disease), and no significance testing between methods.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., 'Task-lavel' typos, somewhat convoluted table/figure presentation) and overall novelty is more of a careful engineering integration of existing components (RAG, GPT-4o planner, SAM adapters, VQA models) than a fundamentally new technical method.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically important problem: making MLLM-based medical diagnosis more evidence-based, interpretable, and grounded in quantitative clinical indicators rather than purely qualitative VQA-style reasoning.

The hierarchical agentic design (task-level planning via RAG-grounded guidelines + case-level execution via specialized tool agents) is a sensible architectural idea that combines retrieval, classical CV/segmentation tools, and LLM reasoning.
The case studies (Figure 1, Figure 3) are illustrative and make the intended benefit of the system (quantitative, criterion-based evidence) easy to understand.
The ablation study on individual vs. combined indicators provides some insight into how indicator quality and decision aggregation affect outcomes.
weaknesses: Extremely narrow empirical validation: only two diseases (glaucoma and heart disease) on two datasets of modest size (1200 fundus images, 536 echocardiograms from 143 subjects), which is insufficient to support the paper's broad claims of a general-purpose 'evidence-based multi-modal medical diagnosis' framework.

The heart disease task is reduced from a 7-class clinically meaningful problem to a simplistic binary healthy/sick classification, substantially weakening the clinical relevance and realism of the evaluation.

The MOE decider's weights w_i and threshold θ are not clearly specified as learned, validated, or held out — it is unclear whether these were tuned on the test set itself, raising serious concerns about overfitting/leakage and inflated reported gains (90.4% mACC vs. 75.9% for the LLM decider is a large, suspicious gap that is not well explained beyond post-hoc rationalization).

No comparison with existing medical agentic frameworks explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., MDAgents, MMedAgent, MedRAX, KG4Diagnosis) despite these being the most directly relevant baselines; comparisons are instead limited to generic MLLMs and single disease-specific classifiers, which is a weak and somewhat unfair baseline selection that favors the proposed pipeline.

Heavy reliance on proprietary closed-source models (GPT-4o, GPT-o1) for nearly every agent role (planner, orchestrator, coding, summary, decider) raises reproducibility concerns and makes the system costly, non-deterministic, and difficult for others to replicate or audit.

No human clinical expert evaluation or validation of the generated 'evidence-based' reasoning chains, despite interpretability/reliability being the central claimed contribution; the paper only offers anecdotal case studies rather than systematic expert review of correctness/faithfulness of the generated explanations.

The pipeline depends on substantial manual/engineering effort per disease (task-specific segmentation adapters, disease-specific tool selection, hand-crafted indicator sets such as vCDR/RT/PPA/DH), undermining the claimed generality and scalability of the framework to new diseases without significant additional engineering.

Statistical rigor is lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-run variance reporting (aside from the ad hoc 10x slice-sampling for MLLM baselines on 3D data), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust.
The writing contains repeated typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'task-lavel', 'Augumented', 'drance hemorrhages', '-cased' instead of '-based') that suggest insufficient proofreading.

The comparison in Table 1 penalizes GPT-4o for 'refusing' to answer with a dash rather than a principled accuracy score, which can bias the comparison in favor of the proposed system and obscures a fair quantitative comparison.

The contribution over prior interpretable/VQA-grounded medical AI approaches (e.g., region-grounded explanation methods cited in related work) is incremental in the sense that chaining existing tools (SAM adapters, VQA models, RAG) via an LLM orchestrator is a relatively straightforward application of known agentic patterns rather than a fundamentally new technical method.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: general MLLMs lack quantitative, evidence-grounded reasoning required for clinical diagnosis, and the paper clearly illustrates this with concrete failure cases (Figure 1).

The hierarchical task-level/case-level agentic design is well thought out, cleanly separating knowledge-based planning (RAG + planner) from case-specific execution (orchestrator, tool agents, coding agent, decider), which is a sensible decomposition of the diagnostic process.

Strong empirical improvements over both general-purpose MLLMs (GPT-4o, LLaVa-Med, Janus-Pro, BioMedCLIP) and, notably, against strong task-specific baselines including REFUGE2 challenge winners and specialized ophthalmology MLLMs (VisionUnite, RetiZero), despite operating largely in a zero-shot/tool-augmented regime.

Comprehensive ablation study (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates the individual and combined contribution of different diagnostic indicators and compares MOE vs. LLM-based decision aggregation, providing useful insight into failure modes of naive LLM decision-making.
Evaluation spans two structurally different modalities (2D fundus images and 3D echocardiography), showing some generality of the framework beyond a single imaging domain.
The case study (Figure 3) provides a transparent, interpretable walkthrough of the full pipeline, supporting the paper's interpretability claims with tangible evidence rather than just assertion.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to only two diseases/datasets; despite claims of general applicability, no evidence is given for other disease types, modalities (e.g., radiology, pathology, dermatology), or more complex multi-class diagnostic settings, which limits confidence in generalization.

No comparison against other existing medical agentic frameworks cited in related work (e.g., MDAgents, MMedAgent, MedRAX, KG4Diagnosis) that tackle similar problems—only comparisons to single foundation models and task-specific non-agentic baselines are provided, leaving the paper's advantage over competing agent designs unverified.

The MOE decider's weights wi and threshold θ are stated to be assigned by an LLM but the methodology, calibration process, and whether these are tuned/validated on a held-out set (versus the test set itself) are not clearly described, raising concerns about potential data leakage or overfitting in the decision rule.

Despite claiming interpretability as a central contribution, there is no human/clinician evaluation of the generated evidence and explanations—only a single illustrative case study is provided, without any systematic assessment of explanation quality, correctness, or trustworthiness.

Heavy reliance on closed-source GPT-4o/GPT-o1 across nearly every agent role (planner, orchestrator, coding, summary) raises reproducibility concerns and leaves unclear how sensitive the framework's performance is to the choice of underlying LLM.

The segmentation/classification tool agents are fine-tuned with task-specific adapters/data, while comparisons to MLLM baselines are framed as "zero-shot," which is a somewhat unfair or at least under-clarified comparison, since MedAgent-Pro benefits from supervised task-specific components that baselines lack.

The heart disease task is reduced from a 7-class problem to binary classification due to limited data, which simplifies the evaluation and may not reflect the complexity of real multi-class differential diagnosis that the paper motivates as important.

No discussion of statistical variance (e.g., multiple runs, confidence intervals) for the reported accuracy/F1 improvements, particularly given the relatively small dataset sizes (1200 and 536 images).

strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical agentic framework (disease-level planning + patient-level reasoning) that closely mirrors real clinical diagnostic workflows, addressing a genuine gap in existing VQA/agent-based medical diagnosis systems that provide unsupported, empirical answers.

Extensive experimental validation across a very wide range of settings (10+ modalities, 20+ anatomies, 50+ diseases, four distinct datasets: REFUGE2, MITEA, MIMIC, NEJM), with consistent and often large improvements over general VLMs, medical agentic baselines, and task-specific SOTA models.

Thoughtful design choices such as RAG-based guideline retrieval for standardized planning, integration of quantitative tool outputs (segmentation, grounding, coding) for evidence generation, and a step-wise reliability verification mechanism (Continue/Terminate/Complete) that adds interpretability and rigor to the reasoning chain.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of planning, quantitative analysis, and evidence-based reasoning, plus additional analyses on segmentation noise sensitivity and decision-fusion strategies.

Human evaluation with clinical experts on workflow alignment (step-count vs. perceived complexity) and diagnostic quality (five-dimension rating) adds clinical grounding beyond automatic metrics, which is valuable for a paper targeting clinical usability.
Clear illustrative case studies (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) that make the pipeline's reasoning process transparent and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core ideas (RAG for grounding, tool-augmented reasoning, step-wise self-verification/reflection) are individually well-established in the broader LLM/VLM agent literature; the contribution is mainly the specific instantiation and combination for the medical domain rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Some baseline results look questionable (e.g., LLaVA-Med scoring exactly 50.0 bAcc / 0.0 F1 across multiple tasks suggests degenerate outputs, possibly due to poor prompt/task adaptation rather than a fair comparison), raising concerns about whether baselines were optimally configured.

The method's dependence on a curated toolbox of task-specific visual models limits generalizability; the paper's own limitations note that tool availability is scarce for many domains, and NEJM results without tool support show much smaller gains, suggesting the improvements are largely tool-driven rather than from the reasoning framework itself.

Reliability/robustness of the plan generation and evidence verification steps (both driven by GPT-4o) is not rigorously stress-tested—e.g., no analysis of failure cases where the VLM's own judgment of evidence reliability (φ) is itself wrong, which could propagate errors silently.

Human evaluation details are thin (unclear number of clinicians, inter-rater agreement, sample size per condition), limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the qualitative clinical assessment.
Reproducibility is a concern: no mention of code/data release, and construction details of the toolset-to-disease mapping and prompt engineering are not fully specified, making replication difficult.

Comparisons with task-specific models (Table 3) are somewhat cherry-picked/limited (few methods, single metrics per domain) and the zero-shot claim may be less impressive given the extensive tool integration and guideline retrieval essentially injecting task-specific knowledge.

The paper's framing as evidence-based reasoning still fundamentally relies on an LLM to interpret retrieved guidelines, weight indicators, and assess evidence reliability, which reintroduces the same hallucination/inconsistency risks it claims to solve (acknowledged only briefly in limitations).

strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical workflow (disease-level planning + patient-level reasoning) that closely mirrors real clinical diagnostic practice, moving beyond one-hop VQA formulations.
Thoughtful integration of RAG-based guideline retrieval with specialized visual/quantitative tools (segmentation, grounding models) to ground reasoning in both literature and measurable evidence.
Extensive empirical coverage across four datasets (REFUGE2, MITEA, MIMIC, NEJM) spanning 10+ modalities, 20+ anatomies, and 50+ diseases, which is unusually broad for this line of work.

Strong quantitative gains over general VLMs, medical agentic baselines, and even task-specific SOTA models (e.g., REFUGE2 AUC, chest X-ray bAcc), suggesting the framework design choices are empirically beneficial.

Component-wise ablations (planning, quantitative analysis, evidence-based reasoning) and additional analyses (indicator accuracy sensitivity, decision-fusion strategy) help isolate the contribution of each module.
Inclusion of clinician-based human evaluation (workflow step-complexity alignment and multi-dimension quality scoring) adds a layer of real-world validity beyond automatic metrics.
Clear, illustrative case studies (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) that make the reasoning process and evidence trail interpretable.
weaknesses: The entire pipeline (planning, orchestration, reliability-check function φ, final diagnosis) is built on GPT-4o, a closed, non-reproducible model; no open-weight backbone results are shown, limiting reproducibility and generalizability of the claimed gains.

The reliability/termination check (φ) that governs the 'evidence-based reasoning' claim is itself performed by the same VLM whose outputs it is supposed to validate, which is somewhat circular and not critically discussed — there is no analysis of how often φ fails to catch actually erroneous quantitative/qualitative outputs.

The medical knowledge base (MedlinePlus) is a consumer-facing health information resource rather than authoritative clinical practice guidelines (e.g., ACC/AHA, WHO, specialty society guidelines); its adequacy for grounding high-stakes diagnostic plans is not justified or validated against clinician-authored guidelines.

Table 2 (MIMIC) omits comparisons with the medical agentic system baselines (MedAgents, MMedAgent, MDAgent) that are included in Table 1, leaving the comparison on the most clinically realistic multi-disease dataset incomplete.

Risk-score weighting (Eq. 5) is generated by the VLM 'guided by the clinical guideline' but the procedure, calibration, and validation of these weights are underspecified and not benchmarked against clinician-assigned weights.

Human evaluation details are sparse — number of clinicians, inter-rater agreement, sample size per condition, and statistical testing are not reported, making it hard to assess the robustness of the qualitative findings in Fig. 7–8.
No analysis of computational cost, latency, or number of tool/LLM calls, which is important for assessing real-world clinical deployment feasibility of a multi-step agentic pipeline.

Baseline agentic systems (MedAgents, MDAgent) originally designed for text-only tasks are adapted to VQA for comparison, which may understate their true performance and bias comparisons in favor of the proposed method.

The claim of being the 'first' evidence-based agentic paradigm is strong given substantial overlap with prior medical agent literature (MMedAgent, MDAgent, etc.); the novelty delta versus simply adding RAG + tool orchestration + a VLM-based gating step could be articulated more rigorously.
No code/plan artifacts or prompts are released or described in enough detail to reproduce the disease-specific plan generation, reducing reproducibility of a fairly complex multi-stage pipeline.

The framework's dependency on available visual tools is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantitatively characterized (e.g., fraction of NEJM cases without tool support and how performance degrades there is only partially discussed).

strengths: Well-motivated hierarchical agentic workflow (disease-level planning + patient-level reasoning) that closely mirrors real clinical diagnostic practice, addressing a genuine gap in existing VLM/agent-based medical diagnosis systems that produce empirical one-hop answers.

Comprehensive experimental validation across four diverse datasets (REFUGE2, MITEA, MIMIC, NEJM) spanning 10+ imaging modalities, 20+ anatomies, and 50+ diseases, with consistent and often large performance gains over general VLMs, medical agentic baselines, and even task-specific SOTA models.
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of planning, quantitative tool-based analysis, and evidence-based reasoning, showing clear incremental value of each component.
Additional analyses (indicator accuracy sensitivity, decision-fusion strategy comparison) provide useful mechanistic insight into why the method works.

Human evaluation by clinical experts, including alignment of workflow step-counts with perceived diagnostic complexity and multi-dimensional quality ratings, adds clinical credibility beyond pure accuracy metrics.
The evidence-based reasoning paradigm (Continue/Terminate/Complete status per step) is a sensible mechanism for improving reliability and interpretability of multi-step reasoning.
weaknesses: The framework's dependence on a manually curated toolset and predefined operation-description pairs (A) raises questions about scalability/automation to new diseases lacking such tool coverage; this is only partially acknowledged as a limitation.

All experiments use GPT-4o as the sole backbone VLM; no ablation demonstrates that the workflow generalizes across different base VLMs, so it's unclear how much of the gain is architecture-specific vs. backbone-dependent.

Some baseline comparisons (MedAgents, MDAgent) were originally designed for text-only QA and had to be adapted to the multi-modal VQA setting, which may understate their true capability and make the comparison less than fully fair.

Key design choices such as the risk threshold θ and indicator weights W appear to be determined by the VLM itself without independent validation or sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness and reproducibility of the final decision-making step.
Human evaluation methodology details (number of clinicians, inter-rater agreement, blinding procedure) are not clearly reported in the main text, limiting assessment of the evaluation's rigor.
No discussion of computational cost, latency, or number of API/tool calls required per case, which is important for practical clinical deployment given the multi-step agentic pipeline.

The RAG knowledge base (MedlinePlus) and retrieval pipeline are not evaluated in isolation (e.g., retrieval precision/recall for guideline relevance), making it hard to assess how much the RAG component itself contributes versus general LLM planning ability.
